Lives · 1919–2005

Maurice Hilleman

Microbiology & Vaccines · United States · 1919–2005

2 min read1 figure, each sourcedWhere it is contestedCorrected onceUpdated 19 September 2026
On this pageBy the numbersWhere it is contestedCorrectedThe definitive biographyReads across to

If lives saved were the measure of fame, he would be a household name.

If you keep one line

Work can outrun credit and still be worth doing — eight of fourteen childhood vaccines say so.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

A blunt, hard-driving Montana farm boy, Hilleman nearly didn't go to college. He is often called the most productive vaccine scientist who ever lived. He developed more than forty vaccines — measles, mumps, rubella, hepatitis A and B, chickenpox, meningitis and pneumonia among them.

Eight of the fourteen vaccines routinely recommended for children today came from his lab. When his own daughter woke with mumps in 1963, he swabbed her throat, cultured the virus and turned it into the vaccine still used. The strain is named “Jeryl Lynn” after her. During the 1957 flu pandemic he recognized the threat early and pushed industry to produce forty million doses, blunting the outbreak in the United States.

He worked in deliberate obscurity, indifferent to credit. That is precisely why so few people know the name of the man who may have prevented more deaths than anyone in history.

40 millionDoses of vaccine given in the three months after his 1957 warning: J. Cavanaugh Simpson, 'The Man Who Beat the 1957 Flu Pandemic', Scientific American, 19 April 2020; Montana State University, 'The Man Who Saved Millions'

02Where it is contested

Offit is a colleague and a public vaccine advocate, and the book is admiring by design — there is no critical distance here. The frequently quoted 'eight million lives a year' figure is an estimate with a wide range, not a measured quantity.

03Corrected

Corrections are appended, never patched. What was wrong, and what is true now:

№ 15 · Sept 2026 · Six superlatives.

An audit of claims printed as 'first', 'only' or 'most' found six that said more than a source would. Genghis Khan's entry said he forged the largest contiguous land empire in history; it reached that size under his heirs, after his death in 1227. Rockefeller's called his the largest fortune in American history, with no measure attached; by inflation-adjusted wealth it is not, and by share of the economy it has arguably been overtaken. It now says one of the largest. Edward Thorp's said Beat the Dealer was, by his own description, the first book to prove the house edge could be beaten; his own account of the book does not say so. Why Firms Exist said Coase's paper was largely ignored for thirty years; the paper was cited long before it was put to use, and the entry now quotes only what Coase is on record as saying, that it was little more than an undergraduate essay. Maurice Hilleman's and Fritz Haber's entries stated as the house's own finding what are other people's judgments; both are now worded as such.

04The definitive biography

Vaccinated: One Man's Quest to Defeat the World's Deadliest DiseasesPaul A. Offit · 2007

Offit, himself a vaccine inventor, interviewed Hilleman extensively in his final months. Both a biography of an irascible genius and a clear-eyed history of how vaccines are made.
